newsitem.title: UK: Salvors say ruling clears way for new approach.
newsitem.headline: Salvors say ruling clears way for new approach.

text.p: The International Salvage Union (ISU) has said a recent Lords ruling on a salvage case opens the way for all participants in the industry to agree new salvage guidelines.

The House of Lords ruled there should be no element of profit in the calculation of a fair rate for tugs and equipment under the Special Compensation provisions of Article 14 of the Salvage Convention. It ruled on February 7 on the case of the Nagasaki Spirit, which was involved in a collision in the Malacca Strait in 1992.
Arnold Witte, president of the International salvage Union, said in a statement: "All parties must now accept this as the basis of calculation.

"The Lords ruling does not lay down precise guidance for this process, so there remains scope to work together to develop a fair and equitable basis for arriving at the amount of Special Compensation in future cases."
Witte added: "There is disappointment amongst salvors that earlier rulings, which put the salvage industry at a disadvantage in the short-term, have been upheld.

"However, we do have a final decision. It is now up to us, together with shipowners, insurers and the P&I Clubs, to join together and reach a new understanding which ensures that this ruling does not erode the effectiveness of the system of pollution defence incentives put in place by member governments of the International Maritime Organisation."

The ISU said the Lords ruling stated that rates for the use of salvors' equipment would be based on "a fair rate of expense which is to be comprehensive of indirect or overhead expenses and to include the additional cost of having resources instantly available".

The Lords also confirmed that Special Compensation should run for the entire period of the salvage operation, the ISU said. It added that this meant Special Compensation was not vulnerable to claims, during a salvage operation, that Article 14 should not apply when a pollution threat has receded or been removed.
Witte said: "This ruling has had the effect of dramatically reducing the financial exposure of P&I Clubs in relation to Article 14 cases."

According to the ISU the entire P&I community has paid out less than $5 million a year in Special Compensation since the provisions of the Salvage Convention were first incorporated into the Lloyd's form in 1990.
As a result Witte called on P&I Clubs "to hammer out a mutually acceptable accommodation" with the ISU on the value of salvage awards.

"The quicker the discussions begin with the involvement of all interested parties, the sooner we can evolve rates and relationships which will accommodate all parties engaged in a marine casualty," he added. --Paul Berrill Reuters Shipping News +Tel 44 171 542 4087
